2[に]手[しゅ]に 分[わ]かれて 追[お]いかけよう。
Let's split up into two groups and chase after them.

手 · て · Martial arts techniques (技/わざ), shogi moves, sumo tricks, hands in card games, general means, ways, and tricks, as well as groups of people.二手 can be read as ふたて when it's used to refer to two ways, groups, or people, so watch out for that.

In the yard, there are two chickens.
全部[ぜんぶ]で 3[さん]投[とう] する ことが できます。
投 · とう · Throwing actions in sports, like pitching or throwing in baseball, and casting a line in fishing.
ビエトは １９[じゅうきゅう]秒[びょう] 息[いき]を 止[と]めていた。
Viet didn't breathe for nineteen seconds.
秒 · びょう · Seconds. It also can be used for angles, latitude, and longitude. The reading is all kango.
コストコで オムツを ３[さん] 箱[ばこ] 買[か]った。
I bought three boxes of diapers at Costco.

箱 · はこ · Boxes. Pretty much any kind is fine. Boxes of diapers, sponge cake, snacks, tea leaves, etc. The only exception to this is small disposable wooden/cardboard boxes filled with sweets, a meal, or bento. These are counted with 折 (おり). When counting with 箱, use wago or kango for one and two. Sometimes use wago for three boxes, but mostly stick with kango. From four and above, use the kango counting method.
漢字[かんじ] コンテストで １[いち]位[い]に なった。
I got first place in the kanji contest.

位 · い · 位 is an ordinal number suffix that's used for classes, grades, ranks, decimal places, and orders (as in the result of a competition or race—this is actually its most common use case). You can also append the ordinal number prefix 第 onto it, as long as you note that it won't take the ordinal number suffix 目. Technically, it can also count the souls and ghosts of the deceased, though that's not common at all.
今日[きょう]は トマト １[いち]玉[たま] ２１[にじゅういち]円[えん]ですって。
I hear one tomato is ¥21 today.

玉 · たま · Round things, such as tomatoes, peaches, heads of lettuce, cabbage, and of course, testicles. It can also be used to count tangled balls of string, and other "ball-shaped" things, even if they're not ball-shaped when taken apart. For example, a ball of yarn could be counted with 玉. Or even a portion of noodles. Instead of 玉, though, it's probably more common to use the general counter 個. One exception to this is pachinko balls, which are pretty much always counted with 玉, no matter what. For one or two balls, use the wago counting method (ひとたま, ふたたま). After that, it's all kango all the way.
１[いち]声[せい] かけてくれれば良[よ]かったのに。
You should have said something to me.

声 · こえ/せい · As a counter, 声 is used to count the number of times you "have a word with someone," as well as the number of times someone or something cries or calls out. This counter uses the wago counting scheme for one and two, but three and above are rare, so focus on ひとこえ and ふたこえ. 声 is part of an idiom worth learning too: もう一声, which means "a little more of a discount." It's handy when you want to barter! 声 (せい) is also used to count the number of sounds, noises, or words that come out of something—usually a mouth. The せい version is counted with kango.
空席[くうせき]は 残[のこ]り ８[はち] 席[せき]と なっております。
There are only eight available seats left.
席 · せき · Seats. In addition to this, it can be used to count meetings or entertainment performances and rankings in a competition or contest.
未読[みどく]の メールが １０００[せん]通[つう]も ある。
There are as many as 1,000 unread emails.

通 · つう · Messages and official documents. Under messages, you get things like emails, letters, comments, telegrams, faxes, answering machine messages, job applications, and survey responses. Under official documents, you have things like bills, reports, licenses, passports, or bankbooks.
2[に] 湯目[ゆのめ]は、と う ふぐ 湯[ゆ]の 足湯[あしゆ]です。

湯 · とう/ゆ · Hot springs, hot spring resorts, onsen.
次[つぎ]の 3[さん] 図[ず]を 見[み]て 問題[もんだい]に 答[こた]えなさい。

ボロネーゼ パスタを １[いち]皿[さら] 注文[ちゅうもん] した。

皿 · さら · 皿 means "dish" or "plate," referring to dishes or plates of food. For empty plates, you can still use 皿, but the counter 枚 will be more common for this. If you want to count individual pieces of food on the plate, you'll want to use 品 (しな). You can use 皿 to count laboratory dishes as well (like the ones that grow bacteria). For one and two plates, use the wago reading (ひとさら、ふたさら). Three can be either (みさら or さんさら). From four on up, just use kango.
この 記事[きじ]を 読[よ]むのに １０日[とおか] かかった。

明日[あした]は 社長[しゃちょう]との ２[に]者[しゃ] 面談[めんだん]が あります。

者 · しゃ · The number of people involved or concerned with something. It's also used to count the batters or base-runners in a baseball game.
三[さん]国[こく] 協定[きょうてい]が 結[むす]ばれたのは いつですか？

国 · こく · Country. You may also see 箇国 or ヶ国, which are used when the speaker or writer is emphasizing a single country.

面 · めん · The faces of cubes and other geometric shapes, newspaper pages, monitors, digital signs, game boards, video game stages, sports fields, rinks or rings, fields, masks, etc.
出店[しゅってん]料[りょう]は 1[いち] 区画[くかく]当[あ]たり 1500[せんごひゃく]円[えん]です。
The fee for the food stand is ¥1,500 per lot.
区画 · くかく · Plots of land, divisions of land, a block, etc.
これは 第[だい]２[に]次[じ] 世界[せかい] 大戦[たいせん]の 時[とき]の 写真[しゃしん]です。
These are photos from World War II.
次 · じ · An ordinal number suffix usually combined with the ordinal number prefix 第 (だい), 次 expresses the order of events.
スーパーで アスパラを ３[さん]束[たば] 買[か]いました。
I bought three bundles of asparagus at the grocery store.

束 · たば · Bunch, bundle. Use wago for one and two bunches, either kango or wago for three bunches, and kango for four bunches and up. There's also another Japanese counter for bundles, 把 (わ), but that's for smaller bundles that can be held with one hand. The 把 counter is becoming uncommon and archaic, though.
トーフグは ジェット 機[き]を ２[に]機[き] 持[も]っている。
機 · き · Air transportation means like airplanes, helicopters, and even guided missiles. Another similar counter, 台, is more associated with ground transportation.

階級 · かいきゅう · Class, rank, or grade.
ここを こう いう 風[ふう]に ２[に] 折[お]り してください。
Please fold here twice like this.
折/折り · おり · You can count folded items with 折 or 折り; the two versions are interchangeable.

試合 · しあい · The word 試合 means "game" (generally referring to a sports game). This counter counts these games. You'll especially see this counter used for Japanese sports—foreign sports may use the gairaigo counter ゲーム instead.
ダブル ベッドの 部屋[へや]を ３[さん]室[しつ] 予約[よやく] したいんですが。

何[なん]名[めい]様[さま]ですか？ かしこまりました。 ５[ご]名[めい]様[さま]ですね。

名 · めい · 名 is a counter for counting people that's more polite than the other person counter, 人. Another difference is that 名 can't be used as an ordinal number suffix like 人 can, so don't try to count the first, second, third (etc.) person. With this one, all you can do is count the number of people.

もう 一[いち]度[ど] 校内[こうない]を 1[いち] 周[まわ]り したが、 見[み]つからなかった。

トーフグは 日本[にほん] ダービーで 3[さん]馬身[ばしん] 差[さ]で 2[に]位[い]に 敗[やぶ]れた。

４８０[よんひゃくはちじゅう] 語[ご] 以上[いじょう]、 ５００[ごひゃく] 語[ご] 以内[いない]で エッセイを 書[か]きなさい。
